q: Helen owns a brokerage account payable on death to her son, a house titled in her name alone with no transfer-on-death deed, and a will leaving everything to her daughter. Which asset passes through probate?
choices: The brokerage account, because a POD designation must be probated
The house, because it is titled in her name alone and no transfer-on-death deed exists
None of the assets, because the will is not effective until probated
The brokerage account, because the will controls every asset
rationale: Wrong — a valid POD designation transfers outside probate, so the account does not go through probate.
Correct — sole-name real estate with no transfer-on-death deed generally passes through probate under the will.
Wrong — the will is probated only for assets that are probate assets; the house is one of them, so this is not the right answer.
Wrong — a will controls only probate assets; a POD designation on the account passes outside the will.
explanation: Probate assets: sole-name property without beneficiary designations or survivorship. Non-probate: POD/TOD accounts, joint property with survivorship, retirement plans with beneficiaries, and trust-owned assets.

q: A client's will leaves his entire estate to his second wife. His 401(k) names his first wife as beneficiary and has not been updated. He dies. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The 401(k) goes to the client's estate and passes under the will
The second wife receives the 401(k), because the will governs all assets
The first wife receives the 401(k), because the beneficiary designation controls the account regardless of the will
The 401(k) is split equally between the wives under state law
rationale: Wrong — the designation keeps the account out of the estate, so it does not pass under the will.
Wrong — a will generally does not override a beneficiary designation on a retirement plan.
Correct — a valid beneficiary designation on a 401(k) governs distribution, regardless of what the will says.
Wrong — the account does not split by state law when a valid designation exists.
explanation: Beneficiary designations on retirement accounts and life insurance override the will. Keeping them current matters after a divorce or remarriage.

q: A married man with two children dies without a will. His wife survives him. Under typical intestacy rules in most states, which statement is most accurate?
choices: The estate goes to the state, because intestacy does not recognize heirs
The wife receives everything, because spouses always inherit the entire estate under intestacy
The children inherit everything, because the spouse has no intestate rights
The estate is shared among the spouse and children under the state's statutory formula, with the spouse receiving a defined share
rationale: Wrong — intestate property passes to heirs under statute, not to the state, unless there are no heirs.
Wrong — intestacy does not give a spouse the entire estate in every state; the formula splits the estate with descendants in many cases.
Wrong — a surviving spouse has intestate rights in every state.
Correct — the state's intestacy statute divides the estate among the spouse and descendants under a formula that varies by state.
explanation: Intestacy is governed by state statute, and the split between spouse and children differs by state. Without a will, the court applies that formula.

sub: Types, features, and taxation of trusts
q: A client wants to avoid probate for his real estate in two states and keep his affairs private, and he still wants to control assets during his lifetime. Which tool best fits?
choices: A revocable living trust that holds the real estate and other major assets
An irrevocable life insurance trust
A testamentary trust created inside his will
A joint tenancy with his adult son on all accounts
rationale: Correct — a revocable living trust avoids probate in each state where property is titled to the trust, stays private, and lets the grantor manage assets during life.
Wrong — an ILIT holds life insurance and is irrevocable, so it does not give the grantor control of other assets.
Wrong — a testamentary trust is created by the will and is subject to probate, so it does not avoid it.
Wrong — joint tenancy with a son exposes assets to his creditors and can create gift and control issues, so it is not the best fit.
explanation: A revocable living trust avoids probate for trust-titled assets (ancillary probate can otherwise occur in other states) and does not reduce estate tax.

q: A husband dies in 2026 and leaves his entire estate to his U.S.-citizen wife. His executor does not file a Form 706 for him. Which statement is correct?
choices: The wife cannot use any of his unused exclusion amount, because no Form 706 was filed
The wife can use his unused exclusion amount only if the executor timely files Form 706 with the portability election
The unused exclusion amount expires after one year
The wife's estate can still use his unused exclusion amount, because portability is automatic
rationale: Wrong — the executor can still elect portability by timely filing Form 706, even without a tax due.
Correct — the deceased spouse's unused exclusion amount is available only if the executor timely files Form 706 and makes the portability election.
Wrong — there is no one-year expiration; the question is whether the election was made.
Wrong — portability is not automatic; it requires an affirmative election on a timely filed return.
explanation: Portability (DSUE): the surviving spouse can use the deceased spouse's unused exclusion only with a timely filed Form 706 and the election, even if no tax is due.

sub: Types, features, and taxation of trusts
q: A husband wants his second wife to receive income from a trust for her life, with the remainder going to his children from his first marriage after her death. Which trust is most appropriate, and why?
choices: A charitable remainder trust, because it gives the children a tax deduction
A grantor retained annuity trust, because it removes the assets from the wife's estate
A QTIP trust, because it qualifies for the marital deduction at his death while the remainder passes to his children
A spendthrift trust, because it prevents the wife from transferring her interest
rationale: Wrong — a charitable remainder trust benefits charity as the remainder, not the children.
Wrong — a GRAT is a lifetime planning tool for a grantor, not a way to provide spousal income at death with a remainder to children.

Correct — a QTIP trust gives the spouse income for life, qualifies for the marital deduction, and passes the remainder to the children as the husband directs; the trust is included in the wife's estate at her death.
Wrong — a spendthrift provision protects against creditors, but it does not provide the marital deduction or control the remainder.
explanation: QTIP: income to a surviving spouse for life, a QTIP election for the marital deduction, and the remainder under the grantor's terms. The property is included in the spouse's estate at her death.

sub: Gift, estate, and GST tax compliance and calculation
q: A grandmother wants to pay her granddaughter's private college tuition directly to the university, and she also wants to give the granddaughter $19,000 in cash for living expenses this year. Which statement is correct?
choices: Both amounts are subject to the annual exclusion, so the tuition uses $19,000 of it
Tuition paid directly is taxable, because direct payments count as gifts above the annual exclusion
The grandmother must file Form 709 for the tuition payment, which eliminates the cash gift's exclusion
Tuition paid directly to the school is excluded from gift tax without limit, and the $19,000 cash gift uses the annual exclusion
rationale: Wrong — the direct tuition payment is not subject to the annual exclusion; its exclusion is separate and unlimited.
Wrong — direct payments of tuition are excluded from gift tax when paid to the school, so they are not taxable gifts.
Wrong — a direct tuition payment does not require a Form 709 when it meets the education exclusion, and the cash gift is a separate matter.
Correct — direct tuition payments to an educational institution are excluded without limit under the education exclusion, separate from the annual exclusion for the cash gift.
explanation: IRC §2503(e): unlimited exclusion for tuition paid directly to a qualifying educational institution. Medical payments directly to providers are excluded in a similar way. The annual exclusion is separate.

q: A client holds stock with a very low basis and wants to sell it without an immediate capital gains tax, while providing income to himself for life and leaving the remainder to charity. Which strategy best fits?
choices: A charitable remainder trust, which pays the client an income for life and passes the remainder to charity
A grantor retained annuity trust, which pays the client income and transfers the stock to heirs tax-free
A private foundation funded with the stock, which pays the client an income for life
A charitable lead annuity trust, which pays income to charity and the remainder to the client's heirs
rationale: Correct — a CRT lets the trust sell the appreciated stock without immediate capital gain, pays the client an income stream, and passes the remainder to charity.
Wrong — a GRAT is a family transfer tool and does not provide a charitable remainder.
Wrong — a private foundation does not pay the donor an income stream, and it does not allow the donor to receive the income from a sale in the same way.
Wrong — a CLAT reverses the structure: charity gets the income first and the heirs get the remainder.
explanation: CRT: the trust sells appreciated assets without immediate tax, pays income to the grantor for life or a term, and the remainder goes to charity. The grantor gets a partial income tax deduction.

q: A client wants a document that lets his daughter manage his finances if he becomes incapacitated, and he wants the authority to end at his death. Which document best fits?
choices: A living trust with no successor trustee
A durable power of attorney for finances
A last will and testament
A healthcare proxy
rationale: Wrong — a trust with no successor trustee does not give anyone authority to act if the client becomes incapacitated.
Correct — a durable power of attorney allows an agent to manage financial matters during incapacity; its authority ends at death, and the will and trust then take over.
Wrong — a will takes effect at death and does not give anyone authority during incapacity.
Wrong — a healthcare proxy covers medical decisions, not financial management.
explanation: Durable POA: financial authority during life, surviving incapacity. Its authority ends at death, when the estate plan (will or trust) controls.

q: A married couple owns their home as tenants by the entirety in a state that recognizes this form. Which statement is most accurate?
choices: The home is split equally between the spouses and each share goes through probate
Either spouse can sell the home alone at any time without the other's consent
The home passes to the surviving spouse outside probate, and generally cannot be reached by one spouse's individual creditors
The home passes under the will of the first spouse to die, and creditors can reach it at any time
rationale: Wrong — entireties property is not split and probated; it passes by survivorship.
Wrong — tenancy by the entirety generally requires both spouses to act together, so one cannot sell alone.
Correct — survivorship passes the home outside probate, and individual creditors of one spouse generally cannot reach entireties property.
Wrong — tenancy by the entirety passes by survivorship, not under the will, and it is protected from individual creditors.
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety: survivorship and protection from individual creditors in states that recognize it, available only to married couples.

sub: Types, features, and taxation of trusts
q: A trustee manages a trust for a surviving spouse (income beneficiary) and the couple's children (remainder beneficiaries). The trustee invests heavily in high-yield bonds that maximize income but lose principal value. Which fiduciary duty is most at issue?
choices: The duty to avoid conflicts of interest with the trust's corporate affiliates
The duty of confidentiality owed to the children
The duty of loyalty, because the trustee benefits personally from the investments
The duty of impartiality, because the trustee favors the income beneficiary over the remainder beneficiaries
rationale: Wrong — no corporate affiliate is involved in the facts.
Wrong — confidentiality is not the issue; the question is the balance of benefits between beneficiaries.
Wrong — nothing in the facts says the trustee benefits personally; the issue is how the portfolio balances the two groups.
Correct — a trustee must act impartially between income and remainder beneficiaries, and shifting value toward income at the expense of principal can violate that duty.
explanation: Duty of impartiality: balance the interests of current income and remainder beneficiaries. Under prudent investor rules, the trustee also considers diversification and the trust's purpose.

sub: Types, features, and taxation of trusts
q: A client plans to transfer $3 million of appreciating stock to an irrevocable trust for his children, and he wants to keep the right to receive annuity payments for ten years. Which trust best fits this goal of shifting appreciation out of his estate?
choices: A grantor retained annuity trust (GRAT), which pays an annuity to the grantor for a set term and passes remaining appreciation to the children
A qualified terminable interest property (QTIP) trust, which passes assets to the spouse
A charitable lead annuity trust, which pays annuities to charity and gives the remainder to the grantor
A spendthrift trust, which pays annuities to the beneficiary and protects assets from creditors
rationale: Correct — a GRAT pays the grantor an annuity for a set term, and any appreciation above the IRS hurdle rate passes to the children with little or no gift tax.
Wrong — a QTIP is a marital-deduction trust for a spouse; it does not shift appreciation to children during the grantor's life.
Wrong — a CLAT pays charity first and the remainder to the grantor, which reverses the goal here.
Wrong — a spendthrift provision protects against creditors and does not move appreciation out of the estate.
explanation: GRAT: a retained annuity for a term; if the grantor survives the term, appreciation above the IRS hurdle passes to beneficiaries outside the estate. If the grantor dies during the term, the assets are included.

sub: Gift, estate, and GST tax compliance and calculation
q: A grandfather wants to give $50,000 directly to his grandson, who is the grandson of the grandfather's child. The grandfather's child is still alive. Which tax issue most directly applies?
choices: The gift is taxable only if the grandfather's estate exceeds the exemption
The generation-skipping transfer tax, because the gift skips the child's generation
No tax applies, because gifts to grandchildren are always excluded
The gift is taxed only at the grandson's income tax rate
rationale: Wrong — the gift is not tested against the estate tax exemption at death; the GST rules apply at the time of the transfer.
Correct — a gift from a grandparent to a grandchild skips a generation, so the GST tax applies unless the amount is covered by the GST exemption or the annual exclusion.
Wrong — gifts to grandchildren are not always excluded; the annual exclusion and GST exemption must be used to avoid tax.
Wrong — gift tax and GST tax are not measured by the recipient's income tax rate.
explanation: Generation-skipping transfer tax applies to transfers to skip persons (grandchildren) beyond the GST exemption and annual exclusion. The GST exemption is separate from the gift exemption and matches the estate exemption amount.

q: A business owner dies, and most of his estate is an illiquid closely held business. His estate owes estate tax due within nine months. Which planning tool best addresses the liquidity need?
choices: A will that gives the business to his children
A revocable living trust with no insurance
Life insurance owned by an irrevocable life insurance trust, which provides liquidity to pay the estate tax
A joint checking account with his spouse
rationale: Wrong — passing the business to the children does not generate cash to pay the tax.
Wrong — a revocable trust does not provide cash for estate taxes, and the business remains illiquid.
Correct — insurance owned by an ILIT provides cash outside the estate to pay estate taxes without adding to the taxable estate.
Wrong — a joint account does not solve the liquidity problem for an illiquid business.
explanation: Estate liquidity: life insurance held in an ILIT is a common source of cash to pay estate tax without inflating the taxable estate, plus options like installment payments under IRC §6166.

sub: Types, features, and taxation of trusts
q: A client names his trust as the beneficiary of his traditional IRA. The trust is drafted without special provisions. Which issue is most important to consider?
choices: Naming a trust always disqualifies the IRA from the 10-year rule
Naming a trust makes the IRA immune from estate tax
The trust can receive the IRA with no tax consequences, so no further review is needed
The trust may be treated as a non-person beneficiary with a shorter payout period, which can accelerate income tax on the IRA
rationale: Wrong — the 10-year rule can still apply when the trust is properly drafted, so it is not disqualified by default.
Wrong — the IRA is still included in the estate for estate tax purposes, so naming a trust does not avoid estate tax.
Wrong — a trust beneficiary without look-through provisions can face faster distribution rules and accelerated income tax.
Correct — if the trust does not qualify as a see-through trust, it may be subject to faster payout rules, so the trust must be drafted carefully.
explanation: See-through (look-through) trust rules determine whether a trust beneficiary can use individual payout periods. Poor drafting can accelerate income tax on inherited IRAs.
